 ET Online ​ Bhai Dooj 2026 on November 11: Check Shubh Muhurat, Tilak Timings, Rituals and Significance ​
 Bhai Dooj 2026 , one of the most cherished Hindu festivals celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters, is just eight days away and will be observed on Wednesday, November 11 . Also known as Bhaiya Dooj, Bhau Beej and Yama Dwitiya, the festival falls on the Dwitiya Tithi of Shukla Paksha in the Hindu month of Kartik. On this auspicious occasion, sisters apply a sacred tilak on their brothers' foreheads, perform aarti and pray for their long life, happiness and prosperity. Brothers, in return, express their affection by giving gifts and promising lifelong support.
 Bhai Dooj comes two days after Diwali and marks the conclusion of the five-day Diwali festivities in many parts of India. The festival holds special religious significance as it commemorates the divine bond between Lord Yama and his sister, Goddess Yamuna. With the celebrations approaching, here is everything you need to know about Bhai Dooj 2026, including its date, Dwitiya Tithi timings, auspicious tilak muhurat, rituals and significance.

 Bhai Dooj 2026 Date and Day
Bhai Dooj will be celebrated on November 11, 2026 (Wednesday) . The festival is observed on Kartik Shukla Dwitiya, the second day of the bright lunar fortnight in the month of Kartik.
 Event Date 
 Bhai Dooj 2026 Wednesday, November 11, 2026 
 Dwitiya Tithi Begins November 10, 2026, at 2:00 PM 
 Dwitiya Tithi Ends November 11, 2026, at 3:53 PM 
 Tilak Ceremony Muhurat 1:10 PM to 3:20 PM 
 Auspicious Period Aparahna Kala 
 Note: The above timings are based on the New Delhi Panchang and Indian Standard Time (IST). Local muhurat timings may vary depending on the city.

 Bhai Dooj 2026 Shubh Muhurat and Tilak Time
According to the Hindu Panchang, the most auspicious time to perform the Bhai Dooj tilak ceremony in New Delhi is during the Aparahna period on November 11.
 Bhai Dooj Tilak Muhurat: 1:10 PM to 3:20 PM 
 Duration: 2 hours and 10 minutes 
The Aparahna period is traditionally considered favourable for performing the Bhai Dooj rituals . During this time, sisters apply roli and akshat (rice grains) on their brothers' foreheads, perform aarti and pray for their well-being and longevity. The Dwitiya Tithi begins at 2:00 PM on November 10 and ends at 3:53 PM on November 11. Since the auspicious afternoon period falls within the Dwitiya Tithi on November 11, the festival will be celebrated on Wednesday.

 Bhai Dooj 2026 Significance
Bhai Dooj holds immense religious and cultural significance in Hindu tradition. The festival celebrates the unconditional love, trust, affection and lifelong bond shared by brothers and sisters. It is an occasion to express gratitude, strengthen family relationships and pray for the happiness and prosperity of loved ones.
According to Hindu beliefs, sisters perform the tilak ceremony and pray to God for their brothers' long lives, good health and success. Brothers, in turn, offer gifts and reaffirm their commitment to supporting and protecting their sisters.
The festival is also associated with Lord Yama, the god of death, and his sister Goddess Yamuna. Therefore, Bhai Dooj is also called Yama Dwitiya. Taking a holy dip in the Yamuna River on this day is considered particularly auspicious. Devotees believe that observing the rituals with devotion brings blessings, happiness and protection from untimely death.
 Bhai Dooj 2026 Puja Vidhi and Rituals
Bhai Dooj is celebrated with traditional rituals and prayers that reflect the affection between siblings. Although customs may differ across regions and families, the central tradition remains the same: sisters pray for their brothers' well-being through the tilak ceremony.
Here is a simple traditional puja vidhi:
 Morning preparations: Sisters wake up early, take a bath and prepare for the puja. They clean the worship area and arrange the puja thali with roli, akshat, diya, sweets, flowers and other necessary items.
 Prepare the puja thali: Place a diya, roli, rice grains, sweets, flowers and a sacred thread in the thali. Some families also include coconut and fruits as part of their traditional offerings.
 Perform the tilak ceremony: During the auspicious muhurat, sisters apply a tilak of roli and rice grains on their brothers' foreheads.
 Perform aarti: Sisters perform their brothers' aarti and pray for their long life, good health, happiness and prosperity.
 Offer sweets: Sisters offer sweets to their brothers and may prepare a special festive meal for them.
 Exchange gifts and blessings: Brothers give gifts to their sisters as a gesture of love and appreciation. Both siblings seek blessings and celebrate their relationship.
 Devotees may also worship Lord Yama and Goddess Yamuna according to their family traditions.
 Bhai Dooj Story: The Divine Bond of Yama and Yamuna
According to Hindu mythology, Bhai Dooj is associated with the story of Lord Yama and his sister Goddess Yamuna. The two shared a loving bond, but Lord Yama was often occupied with his responsibilities and could not visit his sister frequently.
One day, Goddess Yamuna invited her brother to her home. Lord Yama accepted her invitation and visited her on Kartik Shukla Dwitiya. Yamuna welcomed him warmly, applied a tilak on his forehead, performed aarti and prepared a delicious meal for him.
Pleased with her affection and hospitality, Lord Yama asked his sister to seek a blessing. Yamuna requested that every brother who visits his sister on this auspicious day and receives her tilak should be blessed with happiness, prosperity and a long life.
Lord Yama granted her wish. Since then, the day has been celebrated as Yama Dwitiya or Bhai Dooj. According to religious beliefs, brothers who receive tilak from their sisters on this day are blessed with protection and well-being.
 How Is Bhai Dooj Celebrated Across India?
Bhai Dooj is celebrated with different names and regional customs across India.
 North India: Known as Bhai Dooj or Bhaiya Dooj, the festival involves applying tilak, performing aarti, offering sweets and exchanging gifts.
 Maharashtra and Goa: It is popularly celebrated as Bhau Beej, with sisters inviting their brothers for a special meal and performing the tilak ceremony.
 West Bengal: The festival is known as Bhai Phonta. Sisters apply a ceremonial sandalwood or other traditional tilak on their brothers' foreheads and pray for their well-being.
 Nepal: The corresponding celebration is known as Bhai Tika and is observed during the Tihar festival. Sisters apply colourful tika and offer blessings to their brothers.
 Despite regional differences in rituals and names, the central message remains the same: celebrating the special relationship between brothers and sisters.
